description: A lightweight sandboxing tool for enforcing filesystem and network restrictions on arbitrary processes at the OS level, without requiring a container.

summary.one_liner: A CLI and library from Anthropic (srt) that runs arbitrary processes under OS-level filesystem and network restrictions without a container.
summary.what_it_does: The tool wraps any command (agents, local MCP servers, bash commands) and enforces read/write path rules and domain-based network allowlists on the process tree. On macOS it generates Seatbelt profiles for sandbox-exec; on Linux it uses bubblewrap with a network namespace removed and traffic routed through host-side proxies over Unix sockets; on Windows it runs the process under a dedicated local account with a Windows Filtering Platform egress fence. HTTP/HTTPS traffic goes through an HTTP proxy and other TCP through a SOCKS5 proxy, both enforcing allow and deny lists with optional port suffixes. Settings live in ~/.srt-settings.json and default to no network access and no writes outside default paths. The README also describes optional TLS termination, request filtering hooks, Unix socket blocking, and a control channel for updating config while a command runs.
use_cases: restrict local MCP server file and network access
limit filesystem access of untrusted processes
allowlist outbound domains for a command
block reads of SSH keys and secrets
run build or test commands with no network
notable: Secure-by-default allow-only network and write policies, with deny-then-allow for reads
Per-platform native enforcement: Seatbelt, bubblewrap with seccomp, and a Windows srt-sandbox account with WFP
Resolved-address check that blocks allowed hostnames from resolving to loopback, metadata, or local interface addresses
Library API with violation attribution, per-command network allow lists, and an ask callback for undecided hosts
Optional experimental TLS termination for inspecting and rewriting HTTPS requests
caveats: Described as a beta research preview whose APIs and configuration formats may change
Linux glob support for filesystem rules is narrower than macOS; wildcards in leading path components are skipped
Unix socket blocking on Linux needs seccomp, which is x64/arm64 only; otherwise sockets are unrestricted with a warning
TLS termination needs Node or Bun 1.4+ and is marked experimental
